Thinking Outside the Classroom

The season of the spider

By Dr. Megan Taylor · October 7, 2026 · 2 min read

There are lots of signs that fall is arriving in the Bay Area. The days are getting shorter. Leaves are beginning to change. And in my family, we start looking for spiders.

Every year around this time, my kids and I search Golden Gate Park for shamrock orbweavers. They’re hard to miss once you know what you’re looking for: often in wait for prey at the center of giant, wheel-shaped webs— where their family name “orbweaver” comes from—these spiders’ large abdomens range in color from pale cream to bright orange, and their long legs are striped with light and dark colors. It’s no wonder local birds often notice them before we do!

I know for some of you, I’ve already lost you.

Spiders make plenty of people uncomfortable. But I’ve always loved them, and over the years my kids and I have made a tradition of getting closer rather than backing away. We find a few orbweavers each fall in the park and think of them as our “pets” for the season, returning regularly to watch them spin webs, grow, and change.

By the time we encounter these adult orbweavers at their biggest and most spectacular, they’re nearing the end of their lives. They’ve reproduced and left behind egg sacs containing the beginnings of another generation. And eventually, the spiders we’ve been watching disappear.

There is something both beautiful and sad about witnessing the cycle.

The natural world gives us countless opportunities to notice cycles of change. Flowers bloom and die. Leaves fall and return. Insects emerge and disappear. A spider reaches the end of its life, but leaves behind hundreds of eggs that will begin the cycle again.

This fall, I encourage you to look for opportunities to notice life changing around you, including the parts that may feel strange, uncomfortable, or even a little scary. Ask questions. Look closer. Come back tomorrow.

You might be surprised by what captures your curiosity.

If spiders still feel like too much of a stretch, perhaps monarch butterflies are more your speed. On October 24, join us for We All Journey (https://www.exploratorium.edu/visit/calendar/we-all-journey), a special day-time event at the Exploratorium exploring another remarkable cycle of life: the monarch’s transformation from caterpillar to butterfly and its annual migration to Mexico, where its arrival often coincides with Día de Muertos. Through art and hands-on activities, families can explore how cultures find meaning in the natural cycles of life, change, and renewal.

Whether it’s a spider or a butterfly, there’s a lot to learn when we take the time to look closely.

Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life.
